summary: RFC 3723 specified IPsec requirements for block storage protocols over IP such as iSCSI, based on IPsec v2. This document updates those requirements for IPsec v3.

eli5.summary: A set of safety rules for storage-over-network was written for an older lock design. This rewrites them for the newer lock.

questions: why was 3des replaced by aes cbc for storage
extended sequence numbers esp high speed
subtitle: Updates the IPsec rules for iSCSI and similar storage protocols to IPsec v3 and retires 3DES as the mandatory cipher.

tldr.problem: RFC 3723 set IPsec requirements for block storage protocols over IP, such as iSCSI, but it was written for IPsec v2 and for the cryptography of 2004.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC says IPsec v3 (ESPv3 and IKEv2) SHOULD be implemented alongside v2, requires extended sequence numbers at 1 gigabit/second and up, makes AES CBC the mandatory cipher instead of 3DES CBC, and raises the Diffie-Hellman size to at least 2048 bits.
tldr.outcome: It is a Standards Track update that applies to RFC 3723 and to every protocol that inherited its IPsec rules. It has not been obsoleted, according to the unit metadata.

today: RFC 7146 is a Standards Track document, published in April 2014. It updates RFC 3723 and sixteen other RFCs, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why RFC 3723 Needed an Update
sections.content:
RFC 3723 specifies IPsec requirements for block storage protocols over IP, such as iSCSI (RFC 3720), based on IPsec v2. Those requirements were later applied to remote direct data placement protocols such as RDMAP. RFC 7146 brings them up to IPsec v3 (RFC 4301 and related RFCs).

IPsec v2 stays mandatory so that existing implementations keep working. IPsec v3 SHOULD also be implemented, which encourages implementers to move forward. The cryptography requirements are shaped by one expectation: block storage protocols can run at multiple gigabits per second.

Changes to RFC 3723 in brief: extended sequence numbers are required, AES CBC becomes the must-implement cipher, 3DES CBC and AES CTR drop to MAY, specific IKEv2 requirements are added, IKEv1 no longer has to use UDP port 500, OCSP is allowed next to CRLs, and the Diffie-Hellman recommendation becomes a minimum of 2048 bits.
sections.eli5: A set of safety rules for sending disk data over a network was written for an older kind of lock. This paper says to use the newer lock too, and it fixes a few rules that had gotten out of date.

sections.title: Which Protocols Are Affected
sections.content:
Because many protocols reused RFC 3723's IPsec rules, this document updates the IPsec requirements of each of them, and only those requirements. The list covers iSCSI (RFC 3720), Fibre Channel over TCP/IP (RFC 3821), iFCP (RFC 4172), the RDMA and DDP family (RFC 5040 through RFC 5044, plus RFC 5045 and RFC 5046), the iSCSI datamover architecture (RFC 5047) and iSCSI corrections (RFC 5048), among others.

RFC 3721 and RFC 5387 are not updated, because their use of RFC 3723 does not involve its IPsec requirements. The new rules also apply to the consolidated iSCSI specification (RFC 7143) and to iSER (RFC 7145).
sections.eli5: Many different storage programs borrowed the same safety rulebook. When the rulebook changes, each program that borrowed it gets the new pages too.

sections.title: ESP and Extended Sequence Numbers
sections.content:
RFC 3723 requires ESPv2 in tunnel mode, with per-packet data origin authentication, integrity and replay protection. This document says implementations SHOULD also support ESPv3 (RFC 4303) in tunnel mode, and the same protections MUST be provided when ESPv3 is used.

The catch at high speed is the 32-bit ESP sequence number. It cannot roll over within a single security association, so a fast link would force frequent rekeying. To avoid that, implementations that can operate at 1 gigabit/second or higher MUST implement extended (64-bit) sequence numbers for ESPv2, and for ESPv3 if supported, and SHOULD use them for all block storage protocol traffic.

For data origin authentication and integrity, HMAC-SHA-1-96 stays a MUST and AES CBC MAC with XCBC extensions stays a SHOULD, now with a required 128-bit key size. Implementations that support IKEv2 SHOULD also implement AES GMAC with 128-bit keys, because GMAC suits hardware implementation better.
sections.eli5: Every packet gets a number, like tickets at a deli. On a very fast link you would use up the small ticket numbers quickly and have to swap locks all the time, so the rules ask for a much bigger ticket roll.

sections.title: Confidentiality Transforms: AES Replaces 3DES
sections.content:
RFC 3723 made 3DES CBC a MUST and AES CTR a SHOULD. This document reverses the picture. 3DES CBC and AES CTR both become MAY. AES CBC becomes a MUST, with 128-bit keys required. Implementations that support IKEv2 SHOULD also implement AES GCM, again with 128-bit keys required. NULL encryption stays a MUST, which allows security associations that give authentication and integrity without confidentiality.

The reason for dropping 3DES is its 64-bit block size. Weaknesses start to appear as the data encrypted under one key nears the birthday bound, which is 32 GiB for a 64-bit block. A multi-gigabit link can pass that quickly, so rekeying would be needed often. The RFC gives the example of rekeying after 3 GiB for a ten-fold safety margin. AES has a 128-bit block, so its bound is 2^68 bytes.

AES CTR was dropped for a different reason: it is no longer the transform most amenable to hardware. That title now belongs to AES GCM, which provides encryption and integrity in one mechanism. AES CTR's security properties did not change.
sections.eli5: The old scrambler gets tired after a certain amount of data and must be reset often. The new scrambler can handle a mountain of data before it needs a reset, so it is the one every device must have.

sections.title: IKEv1 and IKEv2 Key Management
sections.content:
RFC 3723 requires IKEv1 for peer authentication, negotiating security associations and key management. This document adds that IKEv2 (RFC 5996) SHOULD be supported. The ban on manual keying is extended to every IPsec version, because manual keying cannot rekey at high data rates.

Two IKEv1 rules change. When Diffie-Hellman groups are used, a group of at least 2048 bits SHOULD be offered in all proposals, and 1024-bit groups are NOT RECOMMENDED. The requirement to use UDP port 500 is removed so that NAT traversal can work. Perfect forward secrecy is required for IKEv1 Quick Mode, and now also for the IKEv2 CREATE_CHILD_SA exchange.

Deleting a security association (an IKEv1 Phase 2 delete or an IKEv2 INFORMATIONAL exchange) SHOULD NOT tear down the storage connection; a new association is created if more traffic is sent. If both ends support IPsec v2 and v3, v3 is RECOMMENDED. How peers discover which versions the other supports is left to policy administration.
sections.eli5: Before two computers talk secretly they have to agree on a secret key. The rules say to use the newer agreement method, to never type keys in by hand, and to use bigger numbers when swapping secrets.

sections.title: Peer Authentication and Identity Types
sections.content:
These rules are restated for context and are unchanged for IKEv1. Peer authentication with a pre-shared key MUST be supported; certificate-based authentication with digital signatures MAY be. When signatures are used, negotiators SHOULD use Certificate Request Payloads and SHOULD check certificate validity through a CRL or through OCSP before accepting a certificate.

IKEv1 implementations MUST support Main Mode and SHOULD support Aggressive Mode. Main Mode with a pre-shared key SHOULD NOT be used when a peer has a dynamically assigned address, since that forces a group pre-shared key and creates a man-in-the-middle risk.

For identities, ID_IPV4_ADDR, ID_IPV6_ADDR (if IPv6 is supported) and ID_FQDN MUST be supported under both IKE versions. ID_KEY_ID MUST NOT be used, because it is an opaque identifier that does not interoperate among IPsec implementations. The X.500 types ID_DER_ASN1_DN and ID_DER_ASN1_GN SHOULD NOT be used; an identity from subjectAltName is usually better.
sections.eli5: Both sides must prove who they are. They can share a secret password ahead of time or show an official ID card, and the rules list which kinds of name tags are fine and which are not.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC states that its entire subject is security, and that the security considerations of every referenced RFC apply. It singles out the transforms whose requirement levels changed: AES GMAC, AES GCM and AES CBC are new requirements, and 3DES CBC and AES CTR were lowered.

One warning stands out. AES GCM and AES GMAC are both vulnerable to catastrophic forgery attacks if a nonce is ever repeated with a given key.

3DES CBC remains an optional transform that may suit implementations limited to lower speeds, where its rekeying frequency is acceptable. AES CTR remains suitable for general use; its requirement was lowered only because of hardware considerations. Key sizes of comparable strength SHOULD be used within one security association.
sections.eli5: Some of the new locks fail badly if you ever reuse the same one-time number with the same key, so be careful never to do that. The older lock is still allowed for slow connections.
